splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on when actuarial assumptions for calculating employer withdrawal liability from multiemployer pension plans must be finalized. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations because the timing directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay. SCOTUS resolved this split.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability must be selected by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that a plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date, allowing plans to use more current data.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: The circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year. SCOTUS resolved this split.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, extending the period during which violations can be found.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release terms are not tolled during absconding because no statute authorizes such tolling, and courts lack authority to create common-law doctrines extending punishment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: The circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face a categorical bar under § 2244(b)(1) from raising any claim they previously presented in a successive collateral attack, in addition to the requirements of § 2255(h). If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than Congress may have intended. SCOTUS resolved this split.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, categorically barring them from raising any previously presented claim.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that federal prisoners need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law, without the additional categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures, such as mail-in ballot counting deadlines. The outcome could reshape how courts evaluate candidate standing to challenge election rules, affecting voting procedures nationwide. SCOTUS resolved this split.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates for federal office have Article III standing to challenge state election laws before an election takes place based on competitive injury.

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not have Article III standing to challenge election administration rules pre-election absent a concrete, particularized injury.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits have applied different standards for evaluating discrimination claims against business operators, affecting hospitality, retail, and service industries. SCOTUS granted cert to resolve the disagreement and clarify liability and damages standards. SCOTUS resolved this split.

positions.label: Broader liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a broader standard for establishing discrimination liability in business establishments, making it easier for plaintiffs to prevail.

positions.label: Narrower liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a more restrictive standard requiring stronger proof of discriminatory intent or treatment in business establishments.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps agency or Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions that carry criminal sentencing consequences.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether lenity should prevail over deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations of ambiguous provisions affecting criminal liability or sentencing enhancements. This split has deepened after Loper Bright overruled Chevron. The Third Circuit held deference trumps lenity, while the Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, and Eleventh Circuits have held lenity trumps deference.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference takes precedence over the rule of lenity when interpreting ambiguous guidelines provisions with criminal sentencing consequences.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity prevails over agency or Commission deference, preventing agencies from using delegated power to expand criminal liability without going through proper lawmaking processes.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which expands 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, is a valid authoritative interpretation of the Guidelines under Stinson/Kisor.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary expanding 'controlled substance offense' to include conspiracy and other inchoate offenses is entitled to deference, given that the text of § 4B1.2(b) does not mention inchoate offenses. Some circuits defer to the commentary while others hold it impermissibly expands the guideline text. The Commission has since amended the guideline to address this.

positions.label: Commentary is valid and binding
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of the career-offender guideline entitled to deference under Stinson, and that inchoate offenses like conspiracy qualify as controlled substance offenses.

positions.label: Commentary impermissibly expands the guideline
positions.summary: Holds that the text of § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and the commentary cannot expand the guideline's scope, particularly after Kisor narrowed deference to agency interpretations.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: The circuits are deeply split on whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), or whether possessing any single criterion is disqualifying. This affects whether district courts must impose sentences without regard to statutory minimums for certain drug offenses.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria, reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any single criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as distributive or disjunctive in context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the substance is controlled under state law but not under the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the substance to be federally scheduled or whether a state-scheduled substance suffices. The Eighth Circuit holds there is no federal-law limitation, while other circuits require the substance to be federally controlled.

positions.label: State scheduling suffices
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' broadly includes offenses under state law regardless of whether the substance is also controlled under federal law, as there is no textual basis to graft a federal law limitation onto the guideline.

positions.label: Federal scheduling required
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines only if the substance at issue is also controlled under federal law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly impose punishment for the underlying supervised release violation at revocation, or whether revocation sentences may only serve the purposes of supervised release (such as deterrence and public protection).
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether sentences upon revocation of supervised release may be punitive in nature. The Sixth Circuit (under United States v. Lewis) allows district courts expressly to punish defendants for violations of supervised release, while other circuits hold that revocation sentences must serve only the limited purposes of supervised release. Dissenters in the Sixth Circuit flag the circuit as being at the extreme of this split.

positions.label: Punishment permitted at revocation
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly impose revocation sentences as punishment for supervised release violations.

positions.label: Punishment not the purpose of revocation
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences should serve only the purposes of supervised release — such as deterrence, public protection, and rehabilitation — rather than punishing the defendant for the violation itself.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: The circuits are split on whether non-retroactive changes in law can serve as a basis for compassionate release. The Eighth Circuit (in Crandall) and Seventh Circuit (in Thacker) hold that non-retroactive sentencing changes cannot contribute to extraordinary and compelling reasons. Other circuits, and the Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6), take the opposite view. The Seventh Circuit further holds the Commission exceeded its authority in promulgating the contrary policy statement.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether offered alone or in combination with other factors, cannot contribute to extraordinary and compelling reasons for sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A), and the Sentencing Commission exceeds its statutory authority by saying otherwise.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered as part of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, consistent with the Sentencing Commission's policy statement at U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a federal prisoner challenging a BOP decision about conditions of confinement (such as transfer to prerelease custody or application of First Step Act time credits) must proceed via habeas corpus or may bring a civil rights action (e.g., Bivens or APA).
splits.description: The circuits have been split for decades on whether challenges to conditions of confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) must be brought as habeas claims or may proceed as civil rights actions. This split has evolved in the context of First Step Act earned time credits and prerelease custody determinations. The Supreme Court has noted but never resolved this question since Preiser v. Rodriguez.

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive remedy
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to BOP decisions affecting the duration or execution of a sentence, including application of First Step Act time credits and transfer to prerelease custody, must be brought via habeas corpus.

positions.label: Civil rights actions also available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may challenge certain BOP decisions through civil rights actions rather than being limited to habeas corpus, particularly when the challenge relates to conditions rather than the core fact or duration of confinement.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of an asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert their Chapter 13 case to Chapter 7 in good faith under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 belongs to the bankruptcy estate or the debtor. The Ninth Circuit holds that such appreciation inures to the estate, while the dissent notes this creates a circuit split with courts holding the appreciation belongs to the debtors.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7, based on the broad scope of § 541(a).

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtors
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the debtors, consistent with the statutory structure, purpose, and legislative history of § 348(f)(1)(A).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appeal deadline applies to orders denying attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment in criminal cases.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (subject to the civil appeal deadline) or part of the criminal case (subject to the criminal appeal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joins the majority view that the civil deadline applies, but acknowledges a lopsided circuit split on this issue.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, and the civil appeal deadline (60 days when the government is a party) governs.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is part of the criminal case, and the shorter criminal appeal deadline (14 days) governs.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal court documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether orders denying motions to seal medical records in court filings qualify for immediate appellate review under the collateral order doctrine. The D.C. Circuit held that medical privacy is a value of 'high order' warranting immediate review, while other circuits have been more restrictive about applying the collateral order doctrine to sealing orders.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of high order that warrants immediate appellate review of an order denying a motion to seal such information.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that sealing orders are not immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because the privacy interest can be adequately vindicated through other means, including appeal after final judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
